newsitem.title: UK: S.Africa's Mbeki "encouraged" by Euro trade tour.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Mbeki "encouraged" by Euro trade tour.

text.p: A South African delegation touring European Union (EU) countries to gather support for South Africa's stance in forthcoming trade talks has received "strong encouragement", sources close to the delegation said.
South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki stopped off in London on Monday on the last leg of an eight-nation tour which included Germany, Italy, Sweden, Norway, France and Belgium.

He arrived from Dublin for a meeting with British Prime Minister John Major and stressed South Africa needed a better offer from the EU in the coming trade talks if reconstruction was to progress and if the economies of neighbouring countries was not to suffer.

The sources said Mbeki had had a positive response overall in Europe "but the devil is in the detail (of the trade deal". South Africa, which shares open trade borders and a customs union with Botswana, Lesotho, Nambia and Swaziland, has been lobbying EU governments to stand by comitments made initially in 1994 for an equitable trade deal for itself and other countries in the region.

Following Mbeki's visit, the French government commissioned Jean-Francois Dehecq, chairman of the pharmaceuticals firm Sanofi to study how France could increase its presense in the South Africa economy but no specific support was announced. Meanwhile, an unpublished EU-funded report, completed as South Africa prepares to present its full negotiating position in coming weeks, warns of the potentially devastating knock-on costs of the proposed EU-South Africa Free Trade Area. A statement from UK-based ACTSA, the successor organisation to the Anti-Apartheid Movement, said the report projected a loss of over 280 million rand a year in customs revenues for the four countries, with Swaziland standing to lose nearly 10 percent of its annual government revenue.

Proposals in the agricultural sector would have an even greater effect, ACTSA noted. Products subsidised by the EU's Common Agricultural Policy could hit Namibian beef farmers, who sell 70 percent of their total production to South Africa and Swazi sugar exports particularly hard. Sources in the South Africa trade delegation said Mbeki and other ministers were acutely aware of the unequal trade balance with other countries in the region and the long term problem it might create for South Africa. Trade Minister Alec Erwin, the current chair of the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), has been pushing to achieve a trade agreement within the Southern African Development Community within six months.
Special dispensations for Zambia and Mauritius are likely.

A recent South African parliamentary report on the EU trade talks said the government would insist on a deal that "reinforces, rather than undermines efforts to promote regional co-operation and integration."
